analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.94 malware probability, but the supplied n-gram evidence does not independently show cryptojacking behavior. All 20 features push toward cryptojacking, but each SHAP value is small (+0.006 to +0.016). The top contributors are generic x86-64 compiler idioms: stack and register housekeeping (POP SUB, ADD POP, POP PUSH, INC PUSH, DEC PUSH, PUSH SUB), call setup (CALL ADD, LEA CALL, XOR CALL, CALL XOR), and branch or conditional-move patterns (TEST JZ, TEST JS, CMP JNZ, CMP CMOVZ, CMOVZ MOV, XOR CMOVNZ). Fifteen of the 20 n-grams have a relative frequency of 0.000000, so their SHAP contributions come from the model treating their absence as characteristic of the malware class. That reflects a statistical correlation with the training distribution, not an observed behavior. Only five n-grams are present at all (POP SUB and POP PUSH at 0.010309; INC PUSH, POP OR and DEC PUSH at 0.005155), and these are ordinary prologue/epilogue and counter patterns. No function-level locations are listed, and none of the n-grams shows the dense XOR/ROTATE/SHIFT/arithmetic loops or vector-instruction sequences that would point to a hashing routine. The classifier's high score is a reason to investigate further, but this evidence alone is inconclusive.

analysis.recommended_action: Treat as suspicious but unconfirmed. The n-gram evidence is too generic to support a high-confidence verdict, so corroborate with other analysis: check strings and embedded configuration for pool or wallet indicators, inspect network behavior, and review the binary's functions for tight arithmetic or bitwise loops. Also examine why the model keys on absent patterns, since this may point to a training-distribution artifact. Escalate only if dynamic or structural analysis confirms mining behavior.
